subtitle: The four mathematical ideas behind almost every model: optimise by following the slope, describe uncertainty with distributions, and trust averages.

vec.body:
Forget scary maths for a moment, because you already know this: a spreadsheet is already a matrix. A row of a table is a vector; the whole table is a matrix X, with rows as examples and columns as features.

The star operation is the dot product w·x = Σwᵢxᵢ, a weighted sum, and it sits at the heart of linear models and neurons. Try it: w = (2, −1), x = (3, 4) gives 2·3 + (−1)·4 = 2. The matrix product Xw scores every row at once, so one line of code scores a million customers. And the distance ‖a − b‖ measures similarity: close vectors are alike. What is (1, 2, 3)·(4, 5, 6)? Multiply pair by pair and add.
keynotes: A row of a table is a vector; the table is a matrix X with rows as examples and columns as features.
The dot product w·x = Σwᵢxᵢ is a weighted sum, the heart of linear models and neurons; for w = (2, −1) and x = (3, 4) it is 2.
Xw scores every row at once, and the distance ‖a − b‖ measures similarity.

deriv.body:
Imagine standing on a hill with your eyes closed. How do you find the way down? You feel the slope with your feet. That slope is the derivative: f′(x) is the slope, and it points uphill. With several variables the gradient ∇f collects the partial derivatives and points in the steepest-ascent direction.

So to minimise a loss, walk the opposite way. And when you reach the bottom? The ground is flat, so at a minimum the gradient is zero. To reduce a loss, then, move against the gradient.
keynotes: f′(x) is the slope and points uphill.
The gradient ∇f collects partial derivatives and points in the steepest-ascent direction.
To minimise a loss walk the opposite way; at a minimum the gradient is zero.

gd.body:
Now put the slope to work. Gradient descent says: repeat x ← x − η f′(x), where η is the learning rate, the size of your step. Take small steps downhill until you stop going down.

Let’s watch it. For f = x² − 4x + 5 (minimum at x = 2) we have f′(x) = 2x − 4. Starting from x = −1, f′ = −6, so one step gives x₁ = −1 − 0.2·(−6) = 0.2. After 15 steps with η = 0.2, x = 1.99859, almost exactly 2: the ball rolls to the bottom. But change η to 1.1 and the steps overshoot more than they correct, so it oscillates, each step landing further away. Too small is slow; too large is unstable. If your loss grows each step, what is the first thing to fix? Shrink the learning rate.
keynotes: Gradient descent repeats x ← x − η f′(x) with learning rate η.
For f = x² − 4x + 5 with η = 0.2 from x = −1, one step gives x = 0.2 and after 15 steps x = 1.99859.
With η = 1.1 the steps overshoot and it oscillates; too small is slow, too large is unstable.

dist.body:
Life is uncertain, and a distribution is how mathematics describes uncertainty: it assigns probabilities to outcomes. The binomial counts successes in n trials; the Poisson counts events per interval; the normal N(μ, σ²) models measurement noise, the famous bell.

One fact worth carrying in your head: about 95 % of a normal lies within ±1.96σ. In the simulation, that area is 0.95. To compare different scales, standardise: z = (x − μ)/σ. Suppose an exam score is 70, the class mean is 60 and σ = 5. Then z = (70 − 60)/5 = 2, two standard deviations above average. See the shaded area in the figure: that is the probability.
keynotes: A distribution assigns probabilities to outcomes: binomial counts successes in n trials, Poisson counts events per interval, normal N(μ, σ²) models noise.
About 95 % of a normal lies within ±1.96σ.
Standardise with z = (x − μ)/σ: a score of 70 with mean 60 and σ = 5 has z = 2.

clt.body:
Here is a result so remarkable that it feels like cheating. Take any population, however lopsided, and draw samples of size n. The means of those samples are roughly normal, with standard error σ/√n, whatever the population looks like. That is the central limit theorem, and it is why averages can be trusted.

Don’t just believe it; see it. Simulated means of 30 from a skewed exponential population have sd 0.184, versus theory 0.183. A lopsided population, a bell-shaped pile of means. CLT says sample means become approximately normal as n grows.
keynotes: Means of samples of size n are roughly normal with standard error σ/√n, whatever the population.
Simulated means of 30 from a skewed exponential population have sd 0.184 against theory 0.183.
This is why averages can be trusted.

ci.body:
A single number, like “the average is 52”, hides how sure you are. A confidence interval puts honest doubt into numbers: x̄ ± 1.96σ/√n is a 95 % interval.

What does 95 % mean? Run the experiment 40 times. In the simulation 97.5% of the intervals caught the true mean, with half-width 3.92, and the rose-coloured ones missed it. So a 95 % CI means that the method catches the true value about 95 % of the time over repeated studies, not that this one interval has a 95 % chance. Subtle, and worth getting right.
keynotes: In 40 simulated studies 97.5 % of intervals caught the true mean, with half-width 3.92.
A 95 % CI means the method catches the truth about 95 % of the time over repeated studies.
